Kimberly Ballou Kimberly Ballou serves as Chief of Staff for the U.S. Department of Energy’s Office of International Affairs (IA), a role she resumed in June 2026 after previously serving in the position during a period of leadership transition in early 2025. She has more than two decades of experience advancing U.S. international energy policy, global energy security, strategic partnerships, and international cooperation. Throughout her career, Kimberly has held senior leadership positions across IA, including Senior Advisor for Strategic Operations to the IA Assistant Secretary, Acting Director for Asian Affairs, Deputy Director for American Affairs, and Senior Advisor for Mexico, Central America, and the Caribbean. Kimberly has also served in multiple overseas leadership assignments as Acting Energy Attaché and DOE Office Director, including at the U.S. Embassy in Paris, France; U.S. Embassy in Mexico City, Mexico; and U.S. Mission to the OECD in Paris, where she represented DOE and advanced engagement with foreign governments and key multilateral organizations, including the International Energy Agency and Nuclear Energy Agency. pages.text: Kimi Antonelli - the boy 'born in a garage' and made on the track - BBC Sport By Andrew Benson F1 Correspondent This is an updated version of an article first published in August 2026 Kimi Antonelli was 10 when his father Marco first realised the boy sitting on his lap, operating the steering and gears, might have an exceptional talent as a racing driver. The pair were at the Adria circuit in north-east Italy, Marco with his Lamborghini sports car team, Kimi competing in a karting race. It was the end of the day and Marco, a former driver himself, asked his son: "Do you want to try the Lamborghini?" Of course he did. Marco strapped himself and Kimi into the car, belts extended around both. Dad was in charge of the throttle and brake, his son would control the rest. "I couldn't see the track because he was in front of me with a helmet on," Marco tells BBC Sport. "I could only see beside me the marker panels before each corner - 100m, 50m. "We started to drive, step by step, faster, faster, faster. In the end, I pushed like I was alone and I arrived at the braking point at the end of the straight, 320km/h, braked very hard and at the limit. "The car had a lot of oversteer. Kimi controlled the oversteer perfectly, then I went on the throttle, Kimi finished the oversteer, changed gear, and went. "I said: 'OK, stop, because it has now become dangerous.' But when I saw the video, 10 years old, on my leg, oversteer, everything perfect, I said: 'Maybe he has something special.'" Search Twitter YouTube Facebook Instagram Flickr LinkedIn Kingman Field Office The BLM Kingman Field Office oversees 2.4 million acres of public land in northwestern Arizona, and is located south and east of the Colorado River. The field office is also home to the historic Route 66 Back Country Byway , as well as the largest wild burro population in the country, located in the Black Mountains. Resources include portions of the Sonoran, Mohave, and Great Basin deserts, with saguaro cactus, greasewood, Joshua tree, sagebrush, chaparral, pinyon-juniper woodlands, and ponderosa pine forests. The field office manages nine wilderness areas, 12 Areas of Critical Environmental Concern, and five river segments under consideration for Wild and Scenic River designations. The field office also manages the Grapevine Mesa/Joshua Tree Forest which is considered a National Natural Landmark and one property listed on the National Register of Historic Places. Promoted to this role in June 2026, Ms. Owens provides senior career leadership, direction, and oversight for NNSA’s comprehensive budget and administrative programs. In this capacity, she manages line programs across Human Capital, Learning and Career Management. She also oversees the Office of International Operations, which manages DOE personnel permanently assigned overseas and serves as NNSA's Advisory board member. Ms. Owens represents Human Capital administrative matters with Congress, the Office of Management and Budget, the Government Accountability Office, and the Office of Personnel Management. Prior to her promotion, Ms. Owens served as the Deputy Associate Administrator for Management. Medio millón de caribúes lo atraviesan en su migración, y sus pisadas se entrecruzan en las dunas esculpidas. El río Kobuk es una vía antigua y actual para el hombre y la fauna. Durante 9,000 años, la gente vino a Onion Portage para atrapar caribúes mientras cruzaban el río. Esta tradición continúa aun hoy en día. Las dunas de Great Kobuk se encuentran a 40 millas (64 km) por encima del círculo ártico; no obstante, ¡la temperatura de verano puede alcanzar los 100 °F (38 °C)! Una de las verdaderas rarezas de Alaska es que, en algunos lugares, la arena puede alcanzar los 100 pies (30 m) de altura. Do these drinks really work? “Functional” beverages make big health claims about their brain-boosting, immunity-strengthening abilities. We asked food science and nutrition experts to weigh in. This image taken at over 20,000x magnification shows the microbial population of a SCOBY, the symbiotic culture of bacteria and yeast that ferments tea to make kombucha. Kombucha is one of several probiotic drinks said to boost gut health, just one category of "functional drinks" that also include drinks that improve cognition and immunity. Phil Westcott From Juneau, to Anchorage, to Nome, and beyond, people in Alaska are often spotted wearing a colorful or patterned hooded garment with a big front pocket. This classic Alaska attire is known as a kuspuk. Kuspuk is an English word based on the Indigenous Yup’ik word “qaspeq” which translates to “cloth over parka.” The original qaspeq was made from gut skin, animal hide, or feathered bird skin to keep the wearer warm and dry—a constant struggle known all too well by those who have live, work, and travel in the arctic. In the 1800s, European whalers brought goods to trade, which included cloth bags filled with flour or sugar. Indigenous (Inupiaq/Yup’ik) women repurposed the cotton flour sacks and sewed a lightweight summer garment that resembled the “over parkas” worn in the winter.Today, kuspuks are often made of colorful or patterned cotton material and are locally hand-made. Kyle Haustveit Kyle Haustveit, Under Secretary of Energy Kyle Haustveit was sworn in as the U.S. Department of Energy's Under Secretary of Energy on May 22, 2026. In this role, Mr. Haustveit provides strategic leadership across several offices dedicated to delivering affordable, reliable, and secure energy to the American people. These include the Offices of Electricity; Cybersecurity, Energy Security, and Emergency Response (CESER); Arctic Energy; Indian Energy; Nuclear Energy; Energy Dominance Financing; Hydrocarbons and Geothermal; and the Power Marketing Administrations. Before joining the U.S. Department of Energy, Mr. Haustveit served in a range of technical and leadership roles at Devon Energy. During his tenure, he led teams that developed and commercialized diagnostic techniques now used globally to optimize hydraulic fracturing and resource development. He later directed an Energy Ventures team focused on investments in next-generation energy technologies, including geothermal, carbon utilization, and produced water treatment. Search Twitter YouTube Facebook Instagram Flickr LinkedIn La Cienequilla Petroglyphs | New Mexico View Map In Full Screen Hundreds of petroglyphs, dating from pre-contact time and the Spanish colonial era, can be found along this mesa above the Santa Fe River. Most of the petroglyphs were placed there by Keresan-speaking Puebloan people living in the area between the 13th and 17th centuries. The descendants of these people now live down the Santa Fe River along the Rio Grande at the Cochiti and Santo Domingo Pueblos. The area is known for the great number of hump-backed flute player images and a great variety of bird figures. The site is also of interest to those tracing the route of El Camino Real de Tierra Adentro, as the ancient road passed along here as well. This short trail provides its hikers a glimpse into the past as well as gorgeous views of the surrounding area. The petroglyphs trail is a 1 mile loop that start at the parking lot as a dirt path and then leads into the rocks that need to be climbed through or over. Laboratory Testing for Diphtheria For Public Health July 31, 2026 Key points Clinical laboratories can use various methods to identify Corynebacterium diphtheriae , but identification alone isn't enough for diagnosis confirmation. CDC uses culture and molecular methods, and a specialized toxin production test to confirm diphtheria diagnoses. Confirmatory testing informs clinical management and public health action to prevent further spread. Stay informed on the latest diphtheria specimen acceptance criteria. Overview Laboratories must follow a series of steps in order to confirm a diphtheria diagnosis: Identifying and isolating C. diphtheriae Detecting the diphtheria toxin ( tox ) gene Showing diphtheria toxin production Confirmation of toxin production is key Toxin-producing strains of C. diphtheriae cause diphtheria. Most U.S. strains that possess the tox gene don't express it or produce toxin. Therefore, tests that identify C. diphtheriae or detect the tox gene but don't confirm toxin production are insufficient to confirm a diphtheria diagnosis. June 11, 2024 Laboratory Testing for Mumps Key points Laboratory testing should be performed if mumps is suspected. Collect buccal swab specimen as soon after parotitis onset as possible. Real-time RT-PCR is the preferred method to confirm mumps; it's more sensitive and specific than serologic assays to detect IgM. The successful detection of mumps virus depends primarily on the timing of collection and quality of the clinical sample. Overview Testing for mumps is an important public health action. The timing of specimen collection can play an important role in accurate test outcomes. At the onset of a suspected mumps outbreak, patients suspected to have mumps should be tested by rRT-PCR to confirm mumps and rule out other possible etiologies. However, once a mumps outbreak is confirmed, jurisdictions should consider alternate strategies to ensure efficient use of resources available for laboratory testing. pages.text: Largest 'Sea Dragon' Fossil Accidentally Discovered in Museum | National Geographic 1:00 Artist's impression of the Ichthyosaurus ILLUSTRATION BY JOSCHUA KNÜPPE Largest 'Sea Dragon' Fossil Accidentally Discovered in Museum The paleontologist who made the discovery was originally at the museum to study a fossil that resembles the Loch Ness monster. By Sarah Gibbens Published August 28, 2017 • 4 min read Sven Sachs, a paleontologist from the Bielefeld Natural History Museum in Germany, was at the Lower Saxony State Museum in Hannover to study an ancient sea reptile when one of the museum's display fossils caught his eye. The specimen had originally been unearthed in the mid-1990s in Somerset, England, but it had remained largely unstudied since. Sachs suspected it was an Ichthyosaurus. Commonly mistaken for a dinosaur, the species was more like a "sea dragon" marine reptile that had a long, flexible body and may have swum like eels. "I found it very extraordinary," said Sachs. "[It was] way bigger than any specimen I had examined." He explained the specimen had previously been labeled as a smaller species within the Ichthyosaurus group. Sachs reached out to Ichthyosaurus expert Dean Lomax from the University of Manchester, and in early 2017 they examined the specimen together, finding it to be a specimen of the species Ichthyosaurus somersetensis . Skeleton of Ichthyosaurus . Photograph by Dean Lomax Their findings, published in the journal Acta Palaeontologica Polonica , describe the largest known specimen of its kind.
